name: New Horizons
first: First flyby of Pluto and its moons; sharpest images of a Kuiper belt world
dispatch: New Horizons had exactly one chance and took it. There was no orbit and no way to slow down — nine and a half years of travel, the fastest launch in history, all converging on a few hours at Pluto, executed by a machine so far away that each command took hours to arrive. It nailed the flyby on 14 July 2015 and overturned the expectation of a dead world: Pluto turned out to have mountains of water ice, a vast heart-shaped glacier of frozen nitrogen still slowly churning, and a young, active surface no one thought a body that small and cold could keep. Then it flew on to Arrokoth, a billion kilometres past Pluto — the most distant world ever seen up close — and it is still going.
description: A nine-year sprint after the fastest launch to date, New Horizons compressed decades of anticipation into one July 2015 day — a world turned from a pixelated blur into mountains of water ice and nitrogen glaciers on Pluto's heart-shaped Tombaugh Regio. The spacecraft later flew Arrokoth, linking the mission to the primordial solar system. Flight arcs in Orrery are direct-transfer teaching models, not the actual Jupiter gravity assist.

events.label: LAUNCH
events.note: Atlas V 551 leaves Earth on a Jupiter-gravity-assist path to Pluto.

events.label: PLUTO FLYBY
events.note: Closest approach to Pluto; high-rate imaging and plasma data flood Earth.
